v.why: With edge 3 removed, edge 5 is a major remaining path into the output node, so deleting it cripples the cell (experiments 70 and 72 show drops of 6 to 75 points).
When edge 4 is already absent, edge 3 carries much more of the signal into node 3, so removing it hurts far more (experiments 82 and 84).
If edge 5 is missing, edge 4 is one of only two inputs to the output node, so removing it is much more damaging (experiment 42: -5.5/-11.8/-15.3).
Without edge 5, node 1 feeds the output only through edge 4, and removing edge 0 cuts off that conv path (experiment 94: drops of 5.5 to 15 points).
Replacing a parameter-free pooling op on the first edge with a 3x3 conv adds learnable capacity where it was missing (experiments 18 and 24 are large gains).
Swapping pooling for a conv on the direct input-to-output edge gains much more than swapping in a conv for a 1x1 conv or for a cell that already has convs (experiments 2 vs 3, 7).
When the cell already has a 3x3 conv on edge 0, an extra conv on edge 5 adds little or hurts (experiments 12 and 13 are negative, versus gains elsewhere).
Turning an absent edge into a conv adds both a new path and learnable capacity, which beats replacing an existing conv (experiment 61 gains 5 to 15 points).
Removing a parameter-free skip costs much less than removing a conv on edge 0, and can even help skip-heavy cells (experiments 87, 95 vs 86, 92).
Pooling on edge 4 contributes little useful signal, so removing it is roughly neutral or positive, unlike removing a conv on edge 4 (experiments 36, 38, 41 vs 42, 43).

I picked these by looking for conditions that separated large effects from small ones in the 99 experiments. Each was also checked against standard NAS-Bench-201 structure: how many paths reach the output, and how much convolution the cell already has. Several rest on only two or three supporting experiments, and the all-skip and all-avg_pool parents inflate some effects, so treat them as hypotheses, not confirmed results.
